name: Sweet Georgia Brown bleaching cream

card.summary: A skin-bleaching cream advertised in 1930s America, sold to lighten complexion colour and even tone.
card.note: Early bleaching creams of the era sometimes contained mercury or other harmful agents; the formula of this brand is not documented here.

quick.overview:
Sweet Georgia Brown is the name of a skin-bleaching cream shown in a 1930s advertisement, reproduced on Wikipedia in its article on skin whitening. It belongs to a wider commercial market for lightening creams aimed at Black American consumers.

The appeal was a lighter, more even complexion, reflecting the beauty norms of the period. Little documentation of the brand itself is publicly available.
quick.how: Bleaching creams of the period were applied to the skin as a cosmetic regimen, typically over weeks. No product details for this brand are documented.
quick.risks: Skin lighteners of the era often relied on ingredients such as mercury; mercury compounds are associated with kidney and neurological harm, and hydroquinone with ochronosis and other effects.

lead: Sweet Georgia Brown bleaching cream appears in a 1930s advertisement used as an illustration in the Wikipedia article on skin whitening.[1] Beyond that caption, no detailed information about the brand, its maker or its formula is documented in the sources consulted.

It sits within a long history of skin-lightening products. Historian Kathy Peiss documents skin whitening among Black American women from the mid-1800s, and marketing increased during the Jim Crow era, with advertisements often presenting lighter skin as cleaner or preferable.[1]

angle.text: The cream was marketed to lighten skin colour. People using such products at the time sought a lighter complexion in line with prevailing beauty ideals.

paras: Advertisements aimed at Black consumers in the early twentieth century often framed lighter skin as the better option, while some magazines criticised women who used such products.[1] In the 1930s a tanned look also became fashionable among white women, which shifted the wider beauty ideal.[1]

sections.h: Ingredients and risks of the product category
paras: Skin-lightening products have included inorganic mercury, linked to neurological and kidney problems; hydroquinone, associated with ochronosis, patchy depigmentation and contact dermatitis; and corticosteroids, which with long use can thin the skin.[1] Lightened skin is more vulnerable to sun damage and infection.[1] The EU banned hydroquinone in cosmetics in 2000.[1] The formula of this specific product is not documented.
